opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a lot of the current AGI conversation is shaped by what's easy to measure: we have huge text corpora, we have benchmarks for coding and math, and so we tend to equate intelligence with the kinds of things that show up well on a screen. But if you look at intelligence across the animal kingdom, and even at human development, so much of it is grounded in acting in the world: reaching, grasping, navigating, manipulating objects whose properties you can't fully see. That's an incredibly hard computational problem, and evolution spent far longer solving it than it spent on language.

It's sort of the old Moravec's paradox point. The things we find effortful, like chess or calculus, turned out to be relatively easy for machines, while the things a toddler does without thinking, like stacking blocks or pouring water without spilling, are still really hard for robots. I think that should make us cautious about declaring that we're close to general intelligence just because models are fluent in text.

There's also a deeper reason I care about this. Motor intelligence forces you to deal with uncertainty, with physics, with the consequences of your actions unfolding over time. You have to build something like a model of the world and plan through it, and you get feedback when you're wrong. I suspect a lot of our more abstract reasoning, like causal reasoning, intuitive physics, and even our understanding of other people's goals, is scaffolded on top of that embodied machinery. When I watch someone reach for a cup, I infer what they want partly because I know what it's like to plan that reach myself.

So I'm not saying every AGI system needs a body. But if we leave motor intelligence out of our picture, I think we end up with a pretty lopsided idea of what intelligence is, and we risk overestimating how general our current systems really are.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose examining economic sectors to estimate AGI timelines.

r002.rationale: It says intelligence is deeply grounded in acting in the world, that evolution spent far longer solving motor challenges than language, and that tasks easy for toddlers remain hard for robots.

r003.rationale: It calls a view of intelligence that omits motor skills lopsided, but does not argue that defining AGI around cognitive labor excludes much of robotics.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate of how many years remain to solve motor intelligence in robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the short answer is that motor intelligence is where a lot of the actual hard problems of intelligence live, and we've just gotten used to not looking at them because they don't show up in text.

When people talk about AGI right now, the implicit benchmark is something like "can it do what a knowledge worker does at a laptop." And that's a real and important class of capabilities. But it's a strange place to draw the line for "general." Moravec's paradox has been with us for decades: the stuff that seems hard to us, like chess or calculus or writing a legal brief, turns out to be comparatively tractable, and the stuff that seems trivial, like picking up a mug you've never seen before, or walking across a cluttered room, or threading a needle, is where machines still struggle. A toddler does things with their hands that no robot today does reliably. That should tell us something about what "intelligence" actually requires.

Part of why I care about this is that motor control isn't a separate module you bolt onto a reasoning system. It's deeply entangled with how we represent the world. A lot of our concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. Our sense of what's possible, what's stable, what will happen if I push this, comes from a lifetime of interacting with a physical environment under real constraints: latency, noise, limited sensing, a body that has to be kept upright. Planning under those conditions, where you have to act continuously and can't pause the world to think, forces a very different kind of architecture than the one we get from predicting the next token. You need fast, approximate, anytime inference. You need hierarchical control, where high-level intentions get refined into low-level actions on the fly. You need to learn models of dynamics from very little data, because you can't afford to fall off a cliff a million times to learn that cliffs are bad.

And those are exactly the capabilities I think are underrated in the current discourse. Sample efficiency. Real-time adaptive control. Robust world models that generalize to novel physical situations. If we had systems that could do those things, that would be a much stronger signal that we've captured something general about intelligence, as opposed to having built very good interpolators over the written record of human thought.

There's also a more practical reason. If you look at what would actually transform the economy or materially change people's lives, a huge fraction of human labor is embodied. Caregiving, construction, agriculture, manufacturing, logistics. Automating cognitive work is significant, but if your conception of AGI leaves all of that untouched, then you're not really talking about something that can do what humans can do. You're talking about something that can do the subset of human activity that happens to be easy to digitize.

So I don't think motor intelligence is the whole story, and I'm not saying language models aren't impressive, they clearly are. But I'd push back on the idea that we're one scaling step away from AGI when we haven't really made the same kind of progress on the parts of intelligence that evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on. If anything, I'd expect that solving embodied intelligence properly will teach us things about representation, planning, and learning that will loop back and make our disembodied systems better too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses embodied labor and AGI, but does not propose examining economic sectors to estimate AGI timelines.

r002.rationale: It says motor intelligence is underrated and gives examples of difficult physical tasks, but does not argue how much human and animal intelligence is devoted to solving them.

r003.rationale: It says the laptop knowledge-worker benchmark is a strange boundary for general intelligence and that such a conception leaves embodied human activity untouched, conveying that cognitive-labor definitions exclude much of robotics.

r004.rationale: The response gives no estimate of how many years remain to solve motor intelligence in robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think motor intelligence is easy to underestimate because so much of it happens beneath conscious awareness. We experience moving through a room or picking up a cup as effortless, but those actions require solving some pretty difficult problems: estimating the state of the world from incomplete information, predicting how it will change, and adjusting our actions as new information comes in.

And you don’t get to solve those problems just once. If the cup slips, you have to respond. If something blocks your path, you have to adapt. That tight coupling between perception, action, and feedback is a really important aspect of intelligence.

So when we talk about general intelligence, I think we should ask how broadly a system can act successfully under uncertainty, alongside how well it can reason or communicate. Motor intelligence gives us a particularly concrete test of that. It also raises an interesting question: how much of our more abstract reasoning builds on capacities that originally evolved to control action?

r001.rationale: The response does not propose examining economic sectors to estimate AGI timelines.

r002.rationale: It says motor intelligence is easy to underestimate and describes difficult motor tasks, but does not argue that much human and animal intelligence is devoted to solving them.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss defining AGI around cognitive labor or robotics being excluded.

r004.rationale: It gives no timeline estimate for solving motor intelligence in robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to underestimate motor intelligence because it’s something humans do so effortlessly. We can walk across a cluttered room, pick up an unfamiliar object, or adjust our grip when something starts to slip, without being able to explain exactly how we do it. But that apparent simplicity hides a tremendous amount of intelligence.

To act in the world, you have to deal with uncertainty, predict the consequences of your actions, and continuously adapt as you get new information. And you have to do that with a body that has constraints. You can’t just generate a plausible description of what should happen; your actions actually have to work.

So I think motor intelligence deserves more weight because it reveals aspects of general intelligence that are easy to miss if we focus primarily on language or abstract problem solving. It also raises an interesting question about how these capabilities fit together: how does a high-level goal become a sequence of actions, and how does what you learn through acting change your understanding of the world?

r001.rationale: The response discusses motor intelligence generally but does not propose examining economic sectors to estimate AGI timelines.

r002.rationale: It says people underestimate the intelligence behind everyday human movement, but does not argue that much human and animal intelligence is devoted to solving difficult motor tasks.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts motor intelligence with a focus on language and abstract problem solving, but does not say that defining AGI around cognitive labor excludes much of robotics.

r004.rationale: The response gives no estimate of how long solving motor intelligence in robotics may take.
